stem: Which transaction is recorded in the **general journal**?

options.content: A delivery van bought on credit
options.rationale: Correct: credit purchases of non-current assets go in the general journal.

options.content: Goods for resale bought on credit
options.rationale: These go in the purchases journal.
Cash payments go in the cash book.
These go in the sales returns journal.

explanation: The general journal records transactions that do not fit any other book of prime entry, such as credit purchases of non-current assets.

stem: What is the **narrative** in a journal entry?

options.content: A brief explanation written under the entry
options.rationale: Correct: it says why the entry was made.

options.content: The total of the debit column for the entry
options.rationale: Totals are not narratives.

options.content: The name of the person who made the entry
options.rationale: The narrative explains the transaction, not who wrote it.

options.content: The page number of the ledger account posted to
options.rationale: That is a folio reference.

explanation: Each journal entry ends with a narrative, for example "Shelving bought on credit from Gweru Shopfitters".

stem: Rudo takes goods costing US\$260 from her shop for her own use. Which journal entry records this?

options.rationale: Correct: drawings increase and the goods available for sale (purchases) decrease.
This is the reverse of the correct entry.
The goods were not sold; purchases are reduced at cost.
Drawings are recorded in the drawings account, and purchases rather than inventory are reduced.

explanation: Goods taken for private use: **debit drawings, credit purchases**, at cost.

stem: A customer, Chipo Gumbo, owes US\$410 and has left the country with no chance of payment. Which entry writes off the debt?

options.content: Debit Chipo Gumbo, credit irrecoverable debts
options.rationale: This would increase what she owes.
The sale did happen; the loss is recorded as an expense.

options.content: Debit irrecoverable debts, credit Chipo Gumbo
options.rationale: Correct: the loss is an expense and her account is closed.
No money leaves the bank when a debt is written off.

explanation: An irrecoverable (bad) debt is an expense: debit irrecoverable debts; credit the customer to remove the asset.

stem: In opening entries, how is the **capital** figure found?

options.rationale: Liabilities are owed to outsiders, so they are deducted.

options.content: The bank balance at the start
options.rationale: Capital includes all assets, not just the bank.
This gives a negative of the correct figure.
Correct: capital is the balancing figure, from the accounting equation.

explanation: Assets = capital + liabilities, so capital = assets − liabilities. It is credited in the opening entry.

stem: A journal entry reads: *Debit motor vehicles US\$9,500; credit Kwekwe Motors US\$9,500.* What does it record?

options.content: A vehicle sold on credit to Kwekwe Motors
options.rationale: A sale would credit motor vehicles and debit the buyer.

options.content: A vehicle paid for by bank transfer
options.rationale: A bank payment would be credited to bank in the cash book.

options.content: Repairs to a vehicle owed to Kwekwe Motors
options.rationale: Repairs would be debited to an expense account, not motor vehicles.

options.content: A vehicle bought on credit from Kwekwe Motors
options.rationale: Correct: an asset increases and a liability to the supplier is created.

explanation: Debiting the asset account and crediting a named business means the asset was bought on credit from that business.
hints: Read the entry as a sentence: what increased, and who is now owed?

stem: Farai brings his own lorry, valued at US\$14,000, into his transport business. Which entry records this?

options.rationale: This would reduce both the asset and the owner's capital.
Correct: a non-current asset is introduced as capital.
No money was paid; the owner contributed the lorry.
Drawings are things taken out of the business, not brought in.

explanation: Assets brought in by the owner increase capital: debit the asset, credit capital.
hints: The owner is investing more in the business.

stem: Goods costing US\$300 (selling price US\$420) taken by the owner were recorded as *debit drawings US\$420, credit sales US\$420*. Compared with the correct entry, what is the effect on gross profit?

options.content: Gross profit is overstated by US\$420
options.rationale: This forgets that the correct entry (credit purchases 300) also raises gross profit, by 300.

options.content: Gross profit is understated by US\$300
options.rationale: Recording extra sales raises gross profit; it does not lower it.

options.content: Gross profit is overstated by US\$120
options.rationale: Correct: the wrong entry adds 420 to sales; the correct entry would have cut cost of sales by 300. The difference is 120.

options.content: There is no effect on gross profit
options.rationale: Sales are higher than they should be, so gross profit changes.

explanation: Correct entry: credit purchases 300, so cost of sales falls by 300 and gross profit rises by 300. Wrong entry: credit sales 420, so gross profit rises by 420. Gross profit is therefore $420 - 300 = 120$ too high (and drawings are overstated by 120).
hints: Work out how each entry changes gross profit, then compare.

stem: Every entry in the general journal must have equal debit and credit totals.
explanation: True. A journal entry is an instruction for double entry, so total debits equal total credits.

stem: Credit sales of goods to customers are normally recorded in the general journal.
explanation: False. Credit sales of goods go in the sales journal. The general journal is for transactions that do not fit any other book.

stem: Match each transaction with the account **debited** in the general journal.

left.content: Computer bought on credit for office use
Debt of a bankrupt customer written off
Goods taken by the owner for his family
Old shop counter sold on credit to Tendai
Owner brings her own car into the business

explanation: The account receiving value is debited: the asset bought, the expense, drawings, the buyer who now owes, the asset brought in.

stem: Complete the journal entry for shop fittings costing US\$1,950 bought on credit from Mutare Joinery.
explanation: A non-current asset bought on credit: debit the asset account, credit the supplier.

stem:
Thandeka is opening a new set of books for her Kariba fishing supplies business on 1 January 2025:

| Item | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Premises | 38,000 |
| Equipment | 7,400 |
| Inventory | 5,150 |
| Trade receivables | 2,380 |
| Bank | 1,960 |
| Cash | 240 |
| Trade payables | 3,420 |
| Loan from Mutapa Finance | 8,000 |

Calculate the capital figure to be credited in her opening journal entry.
hints: Separate the assets from the liabilities.

stem: Sipho Mpofu owed Tendai US\$1,275. Sipho's trustee paid US\$480 by bank transfer as a final settlement, and Tendai wrote off the rest as irrecoverable. What amount is debited to the irrecoverable debts account?
explanation: $1,275 - 480 = 795$. The US\$480 received is recorded in the cash book; only the remaining US\$795 is written off.
workedSolution: 1. $1,275 - 480 = 795$. The US\$480 received is recorded in the cash book; only the remaining US\$795 is written off.
hints: Only the part that will never be received is written off.

stem: State **two** reasons why a business uses the general journal.

points.description: To record transactions that do not belong in any other book of prime entry (e.g. opening entries, non-current assets on credit, bad debts, drawings of goods, corrections)
To provide a written explanation (narrative) / authority for unusual entries and reduce errors or fraud

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It gives a book of prime entry for unusual transactions such as opening entries and credit purchases of non-current assets, and its narratives explain each entry so it can be checked later.

explanation: Without the journal, unusual entries would go straight to the ledger with no record of why they were made.

stem:
Chipo owns a pharmacy in Chinhoyi. In March 2025:

| Date | Transaction |
| --- | --- |
| 3 Mar | Bought a laptop and printer for the office on credit from Bulawayo Computers, US\$2,650 |
| 11 Mar | Wrote off the debt of US\$515 owed by Nyasha Banda, who cannot pay |
| 19 Mar | Chipo took goods costing US\$145 (selling price US\$210) for her family |
| 26 Mar | Sold an old display cabinet on credit to Rudo Sibanda for US\$1,800, its book value |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: At what value is the transaction on 19 March recorded?

options.rationale: The goods were not sold; no profit is made on them.
Correct: purchases are recorded at cost, so they are reduced at cost.
No profit is recorded on drawings.
Only the cost is recorded.

parts.explanation: Drawings of goods are at cost.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Prepare journal entries to record the four transactions. Narratives are required.

points.description: 3 Mar: Dr Office equipment 2,650
Cr Bulawayo Computers 2,650
11 Mar: Dr Irrecoverable debts 515, Cr Nyasha Banda 515
19 Mar: Dr Drawings 145
Cr Purchases 145
26 Mar: Dr Rudo Sibanda 1,800
Cr Fixtures and fittings 1,800
Suitable narratives and dates for all four

answerSpec.modelAnswer:

|  | *Laptop and printer bought on credit* |  |  |

parts.explanation: Debit the account receiving value; credit the account giving it.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain the effect of the 11 March entry on Chipo's profit and on her assets.

points.description: Profit falls by 515 (irrecoverable debts is an expense)
Trade receivables (assets) fall by 515

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Irrecoverable debts of US\$515 are an expense, so profit falls by US\$515; trade receivables fall by the same amount.

parts.explanation: Writing off a debt moves it from asset to expense.

explanation: This item tests the main uses of the general journal.
hints: Ask which account gains value and which gives it.
